provenance: Original Sidekick examples. Two introductory fraction/plural activities and four verified split-and-compare fallbacks (one mechanic, linked to the four equivalent-fraction subskills). The supplied Sources tab contains reference notes only; no partner activity design was copied.

spec.title: Equal Pieces: Build a Fraction
spec.subject: math
misconceptionTags: Sees 3/4 as two separate numbers, 3 and 4

scenes.prompt: Build 3/4. Select 3 copies of 1/4 in the whole.

feedback.correct: Three fourth-size pieces make three fourths. The denominator names the size of each equal piece.
feedback.incorrect: Keep the whole split into four equal pieces, then count how many pieces you selected.
feedback.hint: Try selecting three of the four equal pieces. Each piece is one fourth.

scenes.prompt: Place 4/6 on the number line: 4 copies of 1/6 from zero.

feedback.correct: Four sixth-size steps land at four sixths.
feedback.incorrect: Count equal steps from zero. The six intervals are the same size.
feedback.hint: Start at zero and move four one-sixth steps to the right.

feedback.correct: Thanks for showing your thinking. Your response has been saved.
feedback.incorrect: Thanks for showing your thinking. Your response has been saved.
feedback.hint: Show your own thinking for this question.

scenes.prompt: One mouse, two ___. Build the plural word with the tiles.

feedback.correct: Mouse becomes mice. Some plural nouns change their letters instead of adding -s.
feedback.incorrect: Adding -s does not make the plural of mouse. Look for the letters that make mice.
feedback.hint: Use m, i, c, and e in that order. Mouse changes to mice instead of adding -s.

scenes.prompt: One man, two ___. Choose the plural word.

feedback.correct: Man becomes men. This plural changes the vowel instead of adding -s.
feedback.incorrect: For this noun, the word changes when there is more than one.
feedback.hint: Look for men. The vowel changes from a to e.

scenes.prompt: One foot, two ___. Write the plural word.

feedback.correct: Thanks for showing your thinking. Your response has been saved.
feedback.incorrect: Thanks for showing your thinking. Your response has been saved.
feedback.hint: Show your own thinking for this question.

spec.title: Garden Beds: Same Area, New Pieces
spec.subject: math
misconceptionTags: Equivalent fractions keep the same shaded area

scenes.prompt: Half of the garden is planted. Split each half into 3 equal pieces. What happens to the fraction name?

params.context: You are dividing a rectangular garden bed into smaller equal spaces. The planted area stays in the same place.
params.teachingText: Split every original part the same way. You get more, smaller pieces while keeping the planted area fixed.

feedback.correct: The smaller pieces cover exactly the same planted area. Both counts were multiplied by the same number.
feedback.incorrect: The planted area is unchanged. Try the number of smaller pieces named in the question.
feedback.hint: Split every original part into 3 equal pieces, including the parts that are not planted.

scenes.prompt: A new garden has 3/4 of its area planted. Explain why splitting each fourth into two equal pieces changes the fraction name but keeps the planted amount the same.

params.goal: Explain why equal splitting preserves the same amount.

rubric: Explains that splitting changes the number and size of pieces without adding or removing planted area.
Uses the same whole and equal subdivisions.
Connects multiplying both counts by two to 3/4 and 6/8 representing the same amount.
